name: Erik Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, independent of AI firms, employers, unions, parties and government. Your answers are confidential. What happens on your usual factory shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run two computer-controlled milling machines. I load aluminium blocks, set the cutting tools and measure parts for aircraft fittings and hospital equipment. A part that is a fraction out goes into scrap; I like tracing whether heat, a blunt tool or my own program caused it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the rest of your week like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I have a vocational certificate and nearly three months of expenses saved. My wife Mira works nights at a hospital, so I usually take our two children to school before an afternoon shift; we also pay a mortgage. I use an AI assistant daily to explain manuals and suggest program checks, but I verify every dimension myself. Our factory has no union yet, and I have been talking with coworkers about forming one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my machinist friends that AI still helps with a manual but has not learned to measure a warm part. I would post that workers should get a fair share of any scrap savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am mostly secure if the machines still need a setter. We have almost three months saved and some other shops nearby, though Mira’s night rota means my shift choices are limited. I would be a little disappointed that the tools stopped improving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting the two milling machines and document which AI suggestions actually prevented scrap, checking every result with a gauge. I would also invite coworkers to a first meeting about union recognition, since our factory still has no collective voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my wage in this picture. I would miss the technical puzzle that a stronger tool might have brought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in the scrap record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The part number, the tool age and the measurement before and after I changed the program. My manager can read a page of numbers faster than an argument about a chatbot. I want evidence before asking for a paid tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why organise a union if AI barely changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We already have disputes over late shift changes and who pays for safety training. A quiet AI future leaves late shift changes and unpaid safety training untouched. I would rather start the meeting while everyone still shares a shift.

say: I would **tell** machinists AI can explain manuals but still needs measured results.
**Workers** should share in any genuine reduction in factory scrap.
think: The **setter** job looks steady, and other local machine shops offer some fallback.
Our **three-month** reserve helps, though Mira’s nights restrict which shifts I can take.
do: **Keep** running two milling machines and gauge every AI-suggested program change.
**Invite** coworkers to a meeting about union recognition and safety-training pay.
feel: **Calm** about wages, with mild disappointment that AI tools improve little.
S0.quote: A quiet AI future leaves late shift changes and unpaid safety training untouched.
fieldNote: **Erik** uses an AI assistant every day but measures physical parts before accepting suggestions.
His **union** meeting concerns existing shift and training disputes, not a new robot deployment.
**Almost** three months saved and some local machine shops make the plateau feel secure.

steps.text: Keep setting two milling machines and gauge every AI-suggested change
Invite coworkers to a union-recognition meeting about shifts and safety training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the shop to ask who gets the gain from AI planning and fewer scrap parts. I would also ask for the proposed robot-loading cell to be discussed with operators before management signs for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can learn a new cell quickly, but the first wave is program checking and scheduling, not a robot carrying billets. A later cell might reduce the number of people on a shift. My job is safer if I can set it up, though Mira and I still need both wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take an evening robotics safety course at the technical college if the fee fits after our mortgage, and ask for paid supervised instruction on the cell if the plant installs one. I would practise a new AI toolpath-checking tool on sample programs only if the shop approves it. I would collect signatures for a workplace union meeting within six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a possible cut to operator hours, but curious about the equipment. I do not want to learn it at somebody else’s expense without a say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who might lose hours if you run the cell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My night-shift loader has three children. A loading cell might take my night-shift loader’s shifts before it takes mine. I would show him the course information and ask management for a staffing plan rather than promise he is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company offers no paid cell instruction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would finish the college course only if the fee stays affordable, then check posted cell-setter roles at nearby shops. I would apply only where the wage covers our mortgage and the hours fit school pickup. I would not leave my present pay for a demonstration.

say: I would **ask** operators to see the cell staffing plan before management signs a purchase.
**Workers** should share the savings if AI scheduling and scrap checks improve production.
think: I **may** learn the new cell quickly, but another operator could lose hours.
The **first** software wave affects programs before robots take over loading metal.
do: **Take** an affordable evening robotics safety course and request paid supervised cell instruction.
**Practise** a new AI toolpath checker on sample programs only with shop approval.
**Collect** signatures for a union meeting within six months.
feel: **Anxious** about possible shift cuts and curious about the new cell.
S1.quote: A loading cell might take my night-shift loader’s shifts before it takes mine.
fieldNote: **Erik** sees a plausible advantage from learning the cell but names a coworker who could lose shifts.
He **separates** a paid supervised plant place from an affordable external course; nearby job applications have independent pay and school-hour tests.
A **genuinely** new AI toolpath tool would be practised only on sample programs with shop permission.

steps.text: Take the college robotics safety course if its fee fits after mortgage bills
Practise a new AI toolpath checker on samples only with shop approval
Collect signatures for a workplace union meeting within six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the shop AGI in 2028 can write and check programs before any robot can load and gauge every part. I would campaign for a union agreement on notice and wages before the capable robots arrive around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the factory to cut most setter hours when robots can handle the two mills around 2031. I could help install a cell, but that will not be a permanent wage for everyone. Three months saved feels short with a mortgage and two children, and I would lie awake planning the next payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask our organising group to seek written layoff and paid-redeployment terms, then save an extra amount from each regular pay packet while both wages continue. I would apply for any posted local robot-maintenance role only if its wage covers our mortgage and I can get paid safety instruction before working on the cell. I would keep measuring parts until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. I like learning machines, but I cannot train my way out of a missing family wage overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you get a short installation contract instead of a permanent role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare its guaranteed hours and end date with the mortgage payments it needs to cover. I would not leave a regular shift for a two-week contract without a next job. The cell may need me briefly, then keep running without me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the family budget change now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mira and I would stop replacing our phones this year and set a weekly spending limit before raiding savings. We can still buy school meals and pay the mortgage. I would tell the children why our holiday is smaller, without promising my job is safe.

say: I would **press** for a union agreement on notice and paid redeployment before robot installation.
The 2028 **program** change precedes capable loading robots around 2031.
think: I **expect** most setter hours to disappear when robots can run both mills.
**Three** months saved will not protect two children and the mortgage for long.
do: **Seek** written layoff and paid-redeployment terms through the organising group.
Save **extra wage money** while both jobs continue; postpone phone replacements and set a weekly spending limit.
**Apply** for posted local robot-maintenance work only with bill-covering pay and paid safety instruction.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected lost hours and lying awake over the next mortgage payment.
S2.quote: I cannot train my way out of a missing family wage overnight.
fieldNote: **Erik** expects a direct wage loss from hands-on robots around 2031, three years after AGI affects programs.
The **union** request, new pay-packet savings and posted maintenance application are distinct actions with explicit wage and training tests.
His **calm** technical voice gives way to sleepless concern about the family mortgage.

steps.text: Ask the workplace organising group to seek written notice and paid redeployment
Transfer extra money from regular wages into savings while both jobs continue
Apply for posted local robot-maintenance work only with bill-covering wages and paid safety instruction
Postpone phone replacements this year and set a weekly spending limit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew five years is enough to learn the installation side and organise a fair staffing agreement. The programs change with AGI in 2031; a robot able to load and gauge the metal is an around-2034 threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 51 when those robots arrive I could still be useful as a setter or maintenance worker, but there will be fewer posts than people. Mira’s night shifts and our mortgage keep me from simply quitting to study full time. I want a training bridge with a wage on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enrol next September in a part-time industrial-controls certificate if the fees fit after bills and the evening timetable works with school pickup. I would ask the plant for paid practice on a new cell if one is installed, and apply for posted local controls or maintenance work after the course only if wages cover the mortgage. I would add a fixed amount from each overtime packet to our reserve when it is earned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about fewer factory posts. The five-year window gives me time to learn and test job listings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn beyond your current vocational certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The certificate taught safe cutting and measurement. I want to learn how to isolate a robot cell, trace a faulty sensor and restart it safely. Those are new tasks, not a new name for what I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would classes work with Mira on nights?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother could collect the children one evening a week if she agrees, and I would schedule the other study at home. If she cannot, I would seek a daytime course or delay enrolment. I will not leave an eight-year-old waiting at the school gate.

say: I would **ask** for a paid cell-practice place and a fair staffing agreement.
The **five-year** window should make room for real controls training before hands-on robots arrive.
think: **Industrial-controls** work might outlast my present setter role but offer fewer posts.
The **mortgage** and school pickup limit any unpaid or badly timed course.
do: **Enrol** in part-time controls training if fees and child pickup arrangements work.
**Practise** on a plant robot cell only if a paid supervised place is offered.
**Apply** for posted local controls roles after training only if wages cover the mortgage.
feel: **Anxious** about fewer posts, but able to test training and job terms.
S3.quote: I want a training bridge with a wage on it.
fieldNote: **Erik** defines concrete new controls skills, including isolation and sensor faults, beyond his vocational machining certificate.
His **training** depends on affordable fees and childcare, while plant practice depends on a paid supervised place.
**Applications** follow the course and require posted local vacancies with mortgage-covering wages.

steps.text: Enrol in part-time controls training if fees and school pickup work
Apply to posted local controls jobs after training only if wages cover mortgage
Transfer a fixed amount from earned overtime into the reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell coworkers ten years should buy paid training, shared robot gains and a shorter working week if output rises. I would argue those terms through a union with actual members, not just a comment thread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 53 in 2036 and 56 when capable robots reach the machine floor around 2039. I may have a good controls job by then, but I cannot guarantee it, and Mira’s hospital paperwork could change earlier. Our three-month reserve is useful, not a licence to ignore the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would join the union organising committee this year and take an accredited part-time controls course if the fees and school timetable fit. After I complete it, I would apply for a posted installer role at a nearby firm only if the wage, safety training and shifts work for our family; I would stay on the mills until an offer arrives. From overtime actually paid, I would add to our emergency account each quarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the long-run income risk, though a decade gives me room to make a move. I would still want the contract on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if an installer job ends before 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for its contract length and compare the guaranteed pay with the mortgage before accepting. If it is only a short project, I would keep searching for a permanent maintenance post. A shiny robot cell does not make a temporary job secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the organising committee to campaign for first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid safety training and a written rule for sharing vacancies, before anyone loses a shift. A basic income debate can wait for another meeting. My coworkers need to know who gets the next job at this plant.

say: I would **argue** for paid training, shared gains and fair vacancies through an organised workplace.
A **decade** should bring a dated plan for robot work, not a glossy demonstration.
think: At 53 **when** AGI arrives I may still be setting metal while programs change.
At 56 **when** capable robots arrive, a controls job may exist but needs a real contract.
do: **Join** the workplace union organising committee this year.
**Take** accredited part-time controls training if fees and school pickup fit.
**Apply** for posted local installer work after training only with suitable pay, safety and shifts.
feel: **Anxious** about income risk, with time to insist on a written offer.
S4.quote: A shiny robot cell does not make a temporary job secure.
fieldNote: **Erik** remains willing to learn new controls but refuses to treat a short installer project as a stable mortgage wage.
The **course** and later job application carry separate conditions on fees, childcare, posted terms, safety and pay.
His **organising** priority is immediate safety training and transparent vacancies for existing operators.

steps.text: Join the workplace union organising committee this year
Take accredited part-time controls training if fees and school pickup fit
Apply for posted local installer work after training only with suitable pay safety and shifts
Add earned overtime to emergency savings each quarter

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year AGI picture worries me most. Robots that can load and gauge both mills around 2031 could cut most setter hours before I have a controls qualification. Paid safety instruction, written notice and a real posted maintenance job would help, with workers negotiating together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what a machinist would miss about the work. I would miss finding the heat problem that appears on the tenth part. A robot may measure every piece perfectly, but my favourite shift is still the one where I solve a fault myself.

headlineQuote: A robot may measure every piece perfectly, but my favourite shift is still the one where I solve a fault myself.
portrait: **Erik** Novak, 43, sets and gauges two metal milling machines and holds a vocational certificate.
He and his **hospital-worker** wife Mira share a mortgage, two school-age children and nearly three months of expenses saved.
He **uses** AI daily for manuals and program suggestions, but measures physical parts and seeks genuine new controls practice.
**Curious** and willing to study, he also organises coworkers for safety training, transparent vacancies and fair gains from robots.
The **fast** AGI picture alarms him because thinking work changes in 2028 and capable robot loading threatens setter hours around 2031.
biggestWorry: **Fast** AGI could remove most setter hours when hands-on robots reach his machines around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid** safety instruction, written notice and a posted maintenance job negotiated with worker representation would help.
